title: Kinetic Monte Carlo
text:
One possible classification of KMC algorithms is as rejection-KMC (rKMC) and rejection-free-KMC (rfKMC).

### Rejection-free KMC

A rfKMC algorithm, often only called KMC, for simulating the time evolution of a system, where some processes can occur with known rates r, can be written for instance as follows:[1]

Set the time t = 0 .

Choose an initial state k.

Form the list of all N_k possible transition rates in the system r_{ki} , from state k into a generic state i. States that do not communicate with k will have r_{ki}=0 .

Calculate the cumulative function R_{ki}=\sum_{j=1}^i r_{kj} for i=1,\ldots,N_k . The total rate is Q_k = R_{k,N_k} .

Get a uniform random number u \in (0, 1] .

Find the event to carry out i by finding the i for which R_{k,i-1} < u Q_k \le R_{ki} (this can be achieved efficiently using binary search).

Carry out event i (update the current state k \rightarrow i ).

Get a new uniform random number u^\prime \in (0, 1] .

Update the time with t = t + \Delta t , where \Delta t = Q_k^{-1} \ln(1/u^\prime) . Note that this time interval represents the time elapsed between the prior event and this one, rather than the time interval between this event and the next one.[1]

Return to step 3.

(Note: because the average value of \ln(1/u^\prime) is equal to unity, the same average time scale can be obtained by instead using \Delta t = Q_k^{-1} in step 9. In this case, however, the delay associated with transition i will not be drawn from the Poisson distribution described by the rate Q_k , but will instead be the mean of that distribution.)

This algorithm is known in different sources variously as the residence-time algorithm or the n-fold way or the Bortz-Kalos-Lebowitz (BKL) algorithm. The timestep involved is a function of the probability that all events i, did not occur.[1]

### Rejection KMC

Rejection KMC has typically the advantage of an easier data handling, and faster computations for each attempted step, since the time consuming action of getting all r_{ki} is not needed.

On the other hand, the time evolved at each step is smaller than for rfKMC. The relative weight of pros and cons varies with the case at hand, and with available resources.

An rKMC associated with the same transition rates as above can be written as follows:

Set the time t = 0 .

Choose an initial state k.

Get the number N_k of all possible transition rates, from state k into a generic state i.

Find the candidate event to carry out i by uniformly sampling from the N_k transitions above.

Accept the event with probability f_{ki} = r_{ki} / r_0 , where r_0 is a suitable upper bound for r_{ki} . It is often easy to find r_0 without having to compute all r_{ki} (e.g., for Metropolis transition rate probabilities).

If accepted, carry out event i (update the current state k \rightarrow i ).

Get a new uniform random number u^\prime \in (0, 1] .

Update the time with t = t + \Delta t , where \Delta t = (N_k r_0)^{-1} \ln(1/u^\prime) .

Return to step 3.

(Note: r_0 can change from one MC step to another.)

This algorithm is usually called a standard algorithm.

Theoretical[2] and numerical[1,3] comparisons between the algorithms were provided.
